claims.text: CodePipeline's default execution mode is SUPERSEDED.
CodePipeline's SUPERSEDED execution mode locks a stage to one execution at a time.

CodePipeline's SUPERSEDED execution mode only protects an execution once it is actually running, and a newer execution can overtake one that is still waiting to enter a locked stage, dropping it before it starts.

In CodePipeline's SUPERSEDED execution mode, if a CodeBuild stage running `pulumi up` is busy and enough commits land, a queued execution waiting behind it can be superseded and never run, silently skipping a deployment rather than colliding with one already in progress.
Setting a CodePipeline's execution mode to QUEUED causes waiting executions to form a queue so each one runs in turn rather than a later commit erasing an earlier one that never got its turn.
CodePipeline's QUEUED execution mode requires a V2 pipeline.
To use QUEUED execution mode, you must set both the `executionMode` and `pipelineType` when defining the pipeline, either via the AWS CLI's `create-pipeline`/`update-pipeline` commands or as code.
The `aws.codepipeline.Pipeline` Pulumi resource exposes `executionMode` and `pipelineType` inputs.
Using Pulumi ESC to broker short-lived cloud credentials avoids storing provider keys as pipeline variables at all.
When two runs reach the same Pulumi Cloud stack at once, Pulumi Cloud grants the lease to only one of them, and the other run's `pulumi up` fails with an update conflict.
Azure Pipelines can prevent concurrent-run update conflicts at the source with an exclusive lock check on the environment a deployment job targets.
In Azure Pipelines, the exclusive lock check is added from an environment's 'Approvals and checks' tab.
In Azure Pipelines, `lockBehavior` is a setting on the stage that references the environment's exclusive lock check.
The Azure Pipelines `Pulumi@1` task accepts a `command` input (e.g. `up`), a `stack` input, and an `args` input (e.g. `--yes`).
In Azure Pipelines, `lockBehavior: sequential` is not the default; `runLatest` is the default lockBehavior value.

With Azure Pipelines `lockBehavior: runLatest`, only the most recently queued run ever acquires the exclusive lock, so an older run stuck waiting behind it is passed over rather than eventually applied.
Azure Pipelines `lockBehavior: runLatest` is acceptable for a preview environment where only the newest state matters, but not for a stack where every update needs to land.
With Azure Pipelines `lockBehavior: sequential`, every queued stage runs against the lock in order, one at a time.
Azure Pipelines `lockBehavior: sequential` processes queued stages the same way Pulumi Cloud itself serializes updates to a stack.
The exclusive lock check in Azure DevOps can be managed as code with the `azuredevops.CheckExclusiveLock` resource in the Azure DevOps provider.
Pulumi offers native version control integrations for popular Git hosts, independent of TeamCity.
When a Pulumi version control integration is configured, Pulumi Cloud posts infrastructure-change summaries as pull request comments and status checks.
When a Pulumi version control integration is configured, Pulumi Cloud links each stack update back to the commit and pull request that produced it.
If two runs of the same TeamCity build configuration reach the same Pulumi stack at once, Pulumi Cloud grants the update lease to only one of them.
When Pulumi Cloud grants an update lease to one of two concurrent runs targeting the same stack, the other run's `pulumi up` fails with an update conflict.
TeamCity's own default behavior is to let build configurations run concurrently against as many free agents as it has available.
TeamCity does not, by its own default configuration, prevent two concurrent build runs from racing to update the same Pulumi stack.
TeamCity build configurations have an advanced option called 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds', found under that configuration's General Settings.
TeamCity's 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds' advanced option defaults to 0, meaning unlimited simultaneous builds.
Setting TeamCity's 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds' option to 1 causes a second build that would otherwise start immediately to be queued behind the first build instead.
When TeamCity's 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds' option is set to 1, a queued second build runs only once the first build finishes.

Limiting TeamCity's simultaneously running builds to 1 produces the same one-at-a-time behavior that Pulumi Cloud's per-stack lease provides, but applied earlier so the build never reaches the point of hitting the update conflict.
In Azure Pipelines, you can serialize deployments by adding an exclusive lock check to the environment the deployment job targets, with `lockBehavior: sequential` set on the stage.
Azure Pipelines supports an exclusive lock check on an environment as a feature for serializing deployment jobs.
Azure Pipelines has a stage-level setting named `lockBehavior` that accepts a `sequential` value.
AWS CodePipeline has a pipeline-level setting called execution mode that can be set to `QUEUED` so that waiting executions run in turn.
AWS CodePipeline's default execution mode lets a newer pipeline execution supersede an older one that is still waiting to start.
Setting AWS CodePipeline's execution mode to `QUEUED` causes waiting executions to run in turn instead of allowing a newer execution to supersede an older, still-waiting one.
In TeamCity, you can limit concurrent deployment builds by setting 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds' to 1 on the build configuration.
TeamCity has a build configuration setting named 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds'.
